Memory.Wiki's wedge is **cross-AI memory portability** — a structural advantage that giants (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) cannot build.

## The core argument

> "OpenAI는 Claude로 memory deliver 안 한다. Anthropic은 ChatGPT로 안 한다. cross-AI layer는 둘 다 만들 수 없는 구조다."

Each AI vendor is **structurally incentivized NOT to build cross-AI memory**:
- OpenAI shipping memory that helps Claude = a competitive own-goal
- Same logic applies to Anthropic, Google, etc.
- Cross-AI memory can only come from a neutral third party

## Why this is a real moat

1. **Layer 3 (memory protocol) is empty** — Model companies can't enter without sacrificing partner ecosystems; application companies can't define a standard others will follow.

2. **The thesis**: "One URL. Every AI reads it." Users paste `memory.wiki/<id>` into ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini — all fetch the same markdown.

3. **6-12 month window** before closed alternatives ship. First mover defines the standard (like RSS, OAuth, Open Graph).

## The external framing

Internally: "The graph is the product. Cross-AI is the structural wedge giants cannot build."

Externally (to users): "Stop re-explaining your context to every AI."

The internal thesis stays hidden — users see only the pain relief, not the strategic positioning.

Memory.Wiki’s wedge is **cross-AI memory/context portability**.

Single-AI memory systems are closed: ChatGPT Memory helps ChatGPT, Claude Projects help Claude, Cursor rules help Cursor. But users actually work across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and MCP hosts, so they keep re-explaining the same context.

Memory.Wiki sits outside those vendors:

> **One URL. Every AI reads it.**

Its structural advantage is that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc. are incentivized to build memory for their own ecosystems, not a memory layer that also helps competitors. As the hub puts it:

> “OpenAI는 Claude로 memory deliver 안 한다. Anthropic은 ChatGPT로 안 한다.”

So the independent cross-AI layer is the gap giants cannot naturally fill.

Memory.Wiki turns user-authored knowledge into URLs — docs, bundles, and user hubs — that any AI can fetch as markdown/context. The moat is not just storage or retrieval; it is **delivery**: pre-organized knowledge graph/context shipped through a universal URL interface across AI tools.

Based on the 2026-05 product reference, mdfy's core features include:

**Product essence**: Turns any markdown (typed, pasted from AI, or imported) into a clean public URL that humans read in a browser and any LLM (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor) ingests as native context.

**URL architecture (three tiers)**:
- **Doc** (`mdfy.app/<id>`) — single markdown document
- **Bundle** (`mdfy.app/b/<id>`) — ordered set of docs + AI-extracted graph (themes, edges)
- **Hub** (`mdfy.app/hub/<slug>`) — user's whole bundle library + cross-bundle concept ontology

**Editing & rendering**: Tiptap WYSIWYG (Live tab), CodeMirror 6 Source tab, Split view; GFM tables, task lists, footnotes, KaTeX, Mermaid, code highlighting, ASCII diagrams.

**AI integration**: Three-provider failover (Anthropic → OpenAI → Gemini); in-doc actions (polish/shorten/expand/translate); AI side panel; visitor "Ask AI"; concept index/ontology extraction; per-doc and per-chunk embeddings via pgvector.

**Real-time collaboration**: Yjs CRDT over Supabase Realtime, remote cursor presence in both Source and Live panes, up to 5 collaborator avatars with overflow chip, stable per-user colors.

**Permissions**: Three roles (owner/editor/readonly); edit_mode options (owner/account/token/view/public); restricted docs gated by password or sign-in.

**Multi-channel surfaces**: Web (mdfy.app), VS Code extension (v1.4.0), Desktop DMG (v2.2.0, signed/notarized), Chrome Web Store extension, CLI (npm), MCP server (npm), macOS QuickLook plugin.

**Misc**: Dark/light themes, drag-drop import, GitHub repo import, JSON data export, visit log, permanent URLs (no expiry).

Based on the hub content, mdfy's RAG/retrieval works through several layers:

**Storage & indexing (built):**
- **Embeddings**: Per-doc, per-chunk, per-bundle vectors using OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, stored in pgvector (`documents.embedding`, `bundles.embedding`, `document_chunks.embedding`)
- **Chunking**: Heading-aware chunking via `lib/chunk-doc.ts` for finer-grained retrieval
- **Idempotent embeddings**: `embedding_source_hash` skips re-embedding unchanged content

**Retrieval methods:**
- **MCP search (`mdfy_search`)**: Vector similarity search — this is where embeddings earn their keep. Available to MCP hosts (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf) as a native tool
- **Hybrid retrieval**: Vector + BM25 hybrid at paragraph-level chunks (per the personal LLM wiki case study)
- **Semantic Retrieval API** (planned): `?q=react&limit=5` URL parameter for embedding-based chunk search

**Delivery model (the differentiator):**
Rather than traditional RAG, mdfy emphasizes **delivery over retrieval** — the graph (concepts, themes, edges) is pre-built and ships in the URL payload itself, so AI gets pre-organized context instead of querying chunks. Compact mode delivers ~95% token savings vs. concatenating docs.

Core pieces:

4. **Search is semantic, via MCP**

5. **Hybrid recall exists in the memory layer**

6. **URL payloads are not just retrieval**  
   mdfy’s main difference is “delivery, not retrieval”: Bundle and Hub URLs return pre-organized markdown digests with AI-generated graph data, concepts, relations, summaries, and links. The receiving AI often gets the map first, then fetches full docs only when needed.

So: mdfy uses pgvector-backed semantic retrieval internally, but its product thesis is delivering pre-organized context through URLs.

Based on the provided content, mdfy frames its RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline as "mdfy Memory." It performs retrieval using a chunked and hybrid approach (combining vector and BM25 search). 

Here is how the process works:

*   **Embedding & Chunking:** When a document is saved, the embedding pipeline (`/api/embed/<id>`) automatically embeds the title and body for global search. It also breaks the document down into paragraph-level chunks (section-by-section) for finer recall.
*   **Storage:** These embeddings are stored using `pgvector` in a Postgres database across three levels: `documents.embedding`, `bundles.embedding`, and `document_chunks.embedding`.
*   **Retrieval:** LLMs can retrieve this information via the `/recall` API or the `mdfy_search` MCP tool. Instead of relying solely on keyword matches, `mdfy_search` uses semantic vector similarity to find relevant documents and chunks based on meaning.

To optimize costs and avoid unnecessary processing, mdfy uses an `embedding_source_hash` to skip re-embedding content that hasn't changed.

Based on the document "How mdfy keeps your docs, bundles, and hub fresh" (RUMdz2fQ), here's how freshness works across three layers:

**1. Document body — always fresh (automatic)**
- New markdown is in Postgres immediately on save
- Propagates to AI fetches within ~60 seconds
- Edge cache uses `stale-while-revalidate=300` but revalidates in background on changes
- No action needed

**2. Bundle graph — manual "Re-analyze" when stale**
- AI-generated themes/insights are computed once and reused
- Stamped with `graph_generated_at`, compared against members' `embedding_updated_at`
- When a member doc's content changes, bundle becomes stale
- A "Re-analyze with AI" refresh icon appears in the bundle header
- Not auto-rebuilt to avoid wasting LLM tokens during active editing

**3. Hub concept index — automatic + manual top-up**
- Every save enqueues an ontology refresh job (deduplicated)
- Fast-path runs inside Vercel's `after()` closure (finishes in seconds)
- Cron worker backstop if serverless instance dies
- **Guardrails:** 30-min per-doc cooldown + 200-character minimum delta (to control cost)
- A "Re-analyze (N)" banner appears when docs changed since last build
- Clicking it re-extracts only changed docs (capped at 50/click), bypasses cooldown

You can also right-click a doc in the sidebar to **Re-analyze concepts** for a single doc.

The design philosophy: aggressive freshness for body markdown (no clicks), fast-but-not-instant defaults for AI-derived metadata (with explicit override available) — balancing cost discipline with predictability.

mdfy keeps freshness in **three layers**:

1. **Document body — always fresh**
   - When you save a doc, markdown is written to Postgres immediately.
   - `/raw/{id}` and viewer URLs read from the database.
   - AI-facing URLs reflect edits within roughly **60 seconds**.
   - No manual action needed.

2. **Bundle graph — stale-aware**
   - Bundle AI analysis—summary, themes, insights, graph—is generated once and reused.
   - If a member doc changes after `graph_generated_at`, the bundle is marked stale.
   - The bundle URL includes `analysis_stale: true`, so an AI knows the graph may be outdated.
   - Owner sees **“Re-analyze with AI”** and chooses when to refresh.

3. **Hub concept index — automatic + manual override**
   - Every doc save enqueues ontology/concept extraction.
   - Fast path usually updates concepts within seconds.
   - A cron worker retries if the serverless job fails.
   - Guardrails: **30-minute cooldown per doc** and **200-character minimum delta**.
   - If docs changed after the last concept build, the hub shows a **“Concepts out of date”** banner with **Re-analyze (N)**.

So: source markdown stays fresh automatically; AI-derived metadata is refreshed automatically when reasonable, with explicit re-analysis when precision matters.
